name: rebuilt_cover_keeps_the_constraints_but_broken
_the_name_went_through_three_rounds_and_: «tiene» -> «perde» -> «tiene» -> «tiene_ma_rotti». It is not indecision, it is the measurement arriving in pieces. (1) «tiene» (holds) was the hypothesis. (2) A probe showed that ReplaceComponents2 with ReAttachMates: true raises RPC_E_SERVERFAULT and with false goes through, and I DEDUCED that false meant «discard the constraints»: renamed to «perde» (loses). (3) The bench measured 0 lost -- the hypothesis was right, the deduction wrong: renamed to «tiene» (holds). (4) The bench measured 2 PROBLEMS in the document: the constraints are there and are in ERROR. None of the three previous names was true.
_the_lesson_of_the_three_rounds: Two different mistakes, and the second is worse than the first. The first: a probe that tests whether the CALL succeeds does not prove what the call DOES -- it printed the paths and did not count the constraints. The second: having measured that the constraints REMAIN, I concluded that they were fine. **Remaining is not working.** A third question was needed, and it was not about the count: it was about the document.
why: «THE COVER MUST BE REDONE» is the most common gesture of a designer, and entry GA7 named its danger: «if the API replaces the document but does NOT keep the mates, the typical defect shows up again, identical -- different part, no error». The new part goes in, the assembly opens, the rebuild is clean, and the component is free.
_why_the_case_mates_BEFORE_replacing: Because without a mate to lose there is nothing to measure. Step 1 constrains the cover to the base; step 2 replaces it with a different part; step 3 is the state. If the constraints did not survive, «mates_lost» would be greater than zero and the case would say so.
_why_the_signature_had_not_been_found: The census of the APIs looked for it on `IComponent2` -- 170 methods, no ReplaceComponent -- and concluded «it does not list a dedicated signature». It is on `IAssemblyDoc`: ReplaceComponents2(FileName, ConfigName, ReplaceAllInstance, UseConfigChoice, ReAttachMates). It is the same lesson as AddConfiguration3 (note 81s): a name says what a method is called, not on which interface it sits.

expect.why: a constraint to lose is needed: without it, the next step would measure nothing
the new part is INSIDE: you check that some component really uses that file, not the Boolean that ReplaceComponents2 returns
replacing is not adding: the components stay two

THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION OF GA7, measured and not deduced: **the constraints are NOT lost.** `ReAttachMates: false` does not mean «discard them» -- it means «do not try to re-attach them interactively». With `true` and a real constraint to re-attach, ReplaceComponents2 raises RPC_E_SERVERFAULT (measured in four conditions: assembly saved and not, new file open and closed). With `false` it goes through, and the count stays 2 before and 2 after.
expect._and_here_i_was_wrong: I had concluded «the constraints are always lost» from a probe that only tested whether the CALL succeeded: it printed the paths of the components and did not count the mates. The call succeeded, so I had deduced the rest. The bench case measured 0 lost against the 2 I demanded, and it is the case that was right. **A probe that does not measure the thing is not a proof of the thing, not even when it succeeds.**

expect.why: before the replacement the assembly is healthy: it is needed as a reference, otherwise «two problems afterwards» would not say whether they are new

**THE THING THIS CASE FOUND, and it is the defect that gives no error in its pure form.** The constraints SURVIVE the replacement -- the count says 2 before and 2 after, and alone it would say «all fine» -- **but they go into ERROR**, because they pointed at faces of the old part. Two broken constraints that look like two healthy ones. The count of the mates cannot see it: it is `GetWhatsWrongCount` that sees it, the same question a designer asks looking at the red tree.
expect._why_TWO_and_not_one: There is a single constraint, and the problems are two: the mate in error and the component that carries it. We do not demand «greater than zero» but the exact number -- a threshold would let a third problem through that appeared for another reason, and then the case would stop measuring what it says it measures.
expect._if_it_ever_became_0: It would mean that SOLIDWORKS has learned to re-attach the constraints to a replaced part -- good news, and to be verified before believing it. The case would turn red and say so, which is exactly what it must do.

expect.why: THE POINT OF THE OPERATION. The number alone is not enough: whoever reads must know that those constraints ARE THERE and DO NOT HOLD, and what to do -- remove them and put them back. A warning without a remedy is learned to be ignored.

replacing is not adding. The state is re-read after every step, so the expectations on the assembly are here and not in an extra step: a step added only to read the state would have had to use an operation, and PART operations on an assembly are refused.

AND THE CIRCLE CLOSES ON GA5: the state and the operation must tell the SAME thing. The operation says «the constraints remained»; the state, which counts them on its own by re-reading the components, says «every non-fixed component has at least one mate». Two independent readings that agree. If they diverged, one of the two would be lying and we would not know which.
